title: Was Rama right?
hook: a king's duty against Sita's innocence, and why dharma is called subtle
carry: dharma is subtle: even good duties collide
tomorrow: how does the Ramayana end, and who stays behind?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Uttararamacharita and the poets' choices, and your line: hari katha ananta, God's stories never end. Today, the two sides of the argument itself.

A Ramayana play has ended, and a family is still at the dinner table. An uncle says Rama did the right thing: a king belongs to his people first. An aunt puts down her spoon and says Sita did nothing wrong, and she was sent away pregnant into a forest. A teenager asks why nobody asked Sita. Each of them is drawing on the tradition. Today, the strongest form of each side, Sita's own words, and why Hindus have never settled it.
screen: `AFTER THE PLAY, AT THE TABLE.` → `HE WAS A KING FIRST.` → `SHE DID NOTHING WRONG.`

segments.voice: The first side rests on rajadharma, the duty of a king. In this reading, Rama's private life is not his own. A king who keeps what he loves while his people lose faith in him has failed the kingdom, so Rama gives up what is dearest to him, and the poem shows him suffering for it. Readers on this side honor the exile as a terrible sacrifice made by both of them. The second side starts from Sita. She was already tested by fire, in the war book, and found pure. She is pregnant. She is sent away without a hearing, by a husband who knows she's innocent. Readers on this side, devotees of Rama among them, call it a wound in the story. And then there are Sita's own words. When Lakshmana leaves her at the Ganga, Valmiki gives her a message to send back. She knows she is blameless. She carries his child. And she asks Rama to care for the people of the city as he would his own brothers. No shouting; a great deal of dignity. Why can't the tradition settle it? Because Hinduism has a word for this kind of knot. Dharma, right action, is called subtle. In the Mahabharata, when Draupadi asks a hall of elders whether she was lost fairly, the great Bhishma answers that the way of dharma is subtle, and he cannot untie it. Rama's duty as a king and his duty as a husband are both dharma, and here they pull apart. The faith doesn't hide the knot. It keeps both readings inside, and asks you to think.
screen: `RAJADHARMA: THE KING'S DUTY.` · `SITA: BLAMELESS, PREGNANT, UNHEARD.` · `HER OWN MESSAGE BACK TO RAMA.` · `BHISHMA: DHARMA IS SUBTLE.` · then, large: `EVEN GOOD DUTIES COLLIDE.`

segments.voice: Think of a real disagreement with someone you care about. For one breath, argue their side as well as you can; for the next, your own. Go back and forth a few times without picking a winner. If you pray, ask for viveka, clear discernment; if you don't, simply let both sides rest and breathe.
Rajadharma. The king's duty: one real dharma, pulling against another, in a story Hindus still argue over with love.
Your line: dharma is subtle, even good duties collide. Love for the story runs through both sides. Day six hundred sixty-eight.

screen: `DAY 668 COUNTS.` → `DHARMA IS SUBTLE: EVEN GOOD DUTIES COLLIDE.` → `TOMORROW: HOW DOES THE RAMAYANA END?`

howItsDone: Hindu teachers, storytellers and families discuss Sita's exile openly: some defend Rama's choice as a king's duty, some grieve it as a wrong done to Sita, and women's folk songs in several languages sing her side.

original.note: Sanskrit rājadharma: rāja (king) + dharma (duty, right order). the duty a ruler owes the people.

trapdoor: what you thought: either Rama was right or the story is wrong.
what it means: two real duties collided; Hindus call dharma subtle and hold both readings inside the faith.

what a scholar hears: rajadharma is a major theme of Sanskrit epic and law texts, 'dharma is subtle' recurs in the Mahabharata, and Sita's message at the Ganga is one of the places the Uttara Kanda gives her own voice.

Lakshmana.meaning: Rama's brother, who took Sita to the Ganga

dharma.meaning: right action, duty, the right order of things

Bhishma.meaning: the eldest of the Kuru family in the Mahabharata

Draupadi.meaning: the Pandavas' queen, who questioned the elders in the dice hall

viveka.meaning: discernment, telling right from wrong clearly
